structure.title: The family and the parish
structure.text: The opening establishes the Ingmar family and a community whose work, memory, and authority are rooted in the land.

structure.title: The decision to leave
structure.text: Religious conviction reorganises relationships and property. This edition ends with the pilgrims' departure, rather than their later life in Jerusalem.

people.name: The Ingmar family
people.text: An old farming family in a Swedish parish, proud of their name and of always doing what they believe is right in God's eyes.

people.name: Karin
people.text: The eldest daughter of the Ingmar family, who holds the farm together through hard choices about love, duty and inheritance.

people.name: Hellgum
people.text: A preacher back from America who brings a new, demanding faith to the parish and divides families who join him from those who do not.

context.title: Inherited land
context.text: A farm supports livelihoods, family continuity, and status. Selling it alters promises made to people who may not share the seller's faith.
context.takeaway: Property carries relationships as well as value.

context.title: Religious awakening
context.text: A demand for changed life can challenge settled church and household authority. The novel follows how conviction spreads through a community.

notice.text: Notice who must bear another person's sacrifice.
notice.why: An act of faith can transfer costs to others.
Attachment to place becomes more than an abstract tradition.

opening: The farms in this Swedish valley carry generations of work, family pride, and promises about who will inherit. Then a religious awakening persuades some of their owners that God wants them somewhere else. Leaving for Jerusalem sounds like an act of faith until the land must be sold and the people staying behind discover what devotion will cost them. Lagerlöf makes the pull of the ancestral home powerful enough that the decision to abandon it cannot be understood simply as courage or delusion.
